facts.statement: The type specimen of Paracrax antiqua was collected in Weld County, Colorado, in 1871 by Othniel Charles Marsh.
facts.quote: The type specimen, YPM 537, was collected in Weld County, Colorado, in 1871 by Othniel Charles Marsh

facts.statement: Pierce Brodkorb initially classified the remains as a turkey relative (Cracidae) before they were correctly identified as a bathornithid.
facts.quote: It was posteriorly referred to Cracidae by Pierce Brodkorb, before its identity as a bathornithid came to light.

facts.statement: Fossils previously thought to be a cormorant were later reidentified as remains of Paracrax antiqua.
facts.quote: Material previously identified as a cormorant, "Phalacrocorax/Oligocrocorax" mediterraneus, was posteriorly identified as P. antiqua remains.

facts.statement: Paracrax has been synonymized with the names Meleagris antiquus and Phalacrocorax/Oligocrocorax mediterranus.
Paracrax is classified within the family Bathornithidae, though some analyses suggest it may be closer to living seriemas or outside the order Cariamiformes.
facts.quote: Part of Bathornithidae (though some analysis recover it as closer to the living seriemas instead, or possibly entirely out of Cariamiformes)

facts.statement: Paracrax fossils date to the Rupelian stage of the Oligocene and are found in river deposits indicating a savanna-like environment.
facts.quote: Dating to the Rupelian stage of the Oligocene, it is composed of river deposits that showcase the remains of a rich savanna-like environment.

facts.statement: Paracrax lived between 31.8 and 29.5 million years ago during the Rupelian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Rupelian to Rupelian (31.8 to 29.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: Unlike its relative Bathornis which preferred wetter ecosystems, Paracrax inhabited drier environments.
facts.quote: Bathornis, a possible close relative of Paracrax, appears to have favoured wetter ecosystems, while Paracrax occurs in drier environments.

facts.statement: Paracrax possessed a keel that was proportionally shallow, similar to that of ratites.
facts.quote: The keel is rather proportionally shallow, like a ratite's.

facts.statement: Paracrax has unique skeletal characteristics that make it easily identifiable, though these show vague convergence with the modern hoatzin.
facts.quote: It has unique characteristics quite unlike the of any other bird (though vaguely convergent to that of the modern hoatzin), making it easily identifiable.

facts.statement: Paracrax antiqua and P. gigantea were clearly flightless birds with very short forelimbs and keels.
facts.quote: Both P. antiqua and P. gigantea were clearly flightless, being large birds with far too short forelimbs and keels

facts.statement: Paracrax gigantea reached estimated heights of over 2 meters, making it one of the largest bathornithids and the tallest animal in its environment.
facts.quote: Paracrax gigantea in particular is a very large bird, reaching estimated heights of over 2 m, making it among the largest of bathornithids and among the tallest animals in its environment.

facts.statement: Paracrax shared an apex predator role with large mammals like Hyaenodon, Dinictis, and Archaeotherium in its environment.
facts.quote: It is a prime example of a large flightless predatory bird co-existing with large predatory mammals, such as the conspecific Hyaenodon, Dinictis, and Archaeotherium with which it probably shared an apex predator role in its environment.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Paracrax wetmorei was capable of limited flight, unlike its congeners.
facts.quote: though P. wetmorei might have still been capable of limited flight.

rejected.statement: Paracrax had similar body proportions to terror birds, featuring proportionally short wings and a large, deep bill.
rejected.quote: Overall, it can be assumed that it had similar proportions to phorusrhacids, with proportionally short wings and a large, deep bill.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'proportionally short wings and a large deep bill'

rejected.statement: Paracrax likely used its large, axe-like beak to subdue and kill prey.
rejected.quote: using its large axe-like beak to subdue and kill its prey.
